newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle Atlantis heads for Mir despite problem.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle Atlantis heads for Mir despite problem.

text.p: Shuttle Atlantis on Tuesday closed in on the orbiting Russian space station where U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid eagerly awaited her ride home.

The shuttle remained on target to dock with Mir late on Wednesday despite the unexplained and unexpected shutdown of a crucial component in the reusable spaceship's hydraulic system, NASA managers said. Atlantis was to pick up Lucid, in her fifth month aboard the station, and drop off veteran astronaut John Blaha, her replacement, for a four-month stay.
The failure of one of three auxiliary power units shortly after Atlantis reached orbit on Monday would not mean an early end to the flight, NASA officials said on Tuesday.

"At this time we don't really see an impact to the mission," mission operations director Lee Briscoe said. Based on all the data that we had gathered it was agreed by all folks we would continue" for a full 10 days in space.

NASA's flight rules required the mission to be curtailed if one of the devices failed, but a recent change to the rule book allowed the mission to go ahead if shuttle managers "agree that it is a safe and reasonable course of action."

The auxiliary power units are part of the hydraulic system that moves the shuttle's engines, wing flaps and rudder during launch and landing. The devices are not needed in orbit and the shuttle can land safely with just two operational units. A second failure, however, could place the shuttle in danger.
Atlantis was 16,000 miles (25,700 km) from Mir when the astronauts awoke on Monday evening and was closing in on the station by 571 miles (919 km) with every 90-minute revolution around Earth.

The crew of six spent their first full day in space checking out experiments and supplies in a pressurized compartment housed in the shuttle's cargo bay. The so-called Spacehab module was doubled in size for this mission to accommodate more supplies for Mir.
A balky experiment caused the astronauts to fall behind schedule and a test of the shuttle's docking system needed for the linkup with Mir was put off until later on Tuesday.

Atlantis thundered into space before dawn on Monday, ending nearly seven weeks of delays caused by shuttle booster problems, a menacing offshore hurricane and difficulty finding a launch date on the busy schedule at Cape Canaveral.
Lucid caught a glimpse of the shuttle's fiery ascent as Mir sailed through space high above the Kennedy Space Centre. She spent Tuesday getting ready for the shuttle's arrival.

"She's doing some last-minute packing," said NASA spokeswoman Kari Fluegel at Russia's mission control, just outside of Moscow. Atlantis, making its fourth visit to Mir, was due to dock with the orbiting outpost at around 11:13 p.m. EDT on Wednesday (0313 GMT on Thursday).
The shuttle and Mir will remain docked for five days while Lucid and Blaha switch places and thousands of pounds (kg) of equipment and supplies are transferred to and from Mir.
Lucid, a 53-year-old mother of three, was originally due home in early August. She is the first of six U.S. astronauts who will staff the Russian space outpost into 1998.

The shuttle's late arrival gave Lucid an extra entry in the record books for the world's longest space mission by a woman. She had already broken the record for the longest stay in space by an American.
If all goes as planned, Lucid will to return home aboard Atlantis on Sept. 26 after 188 days in space.
